docs.title: Certification overview
docs.text: The AZ-700 exam focuses on designing and implementing Azure networking solutions, including hybrid connectivity, routing, security, load balancing, monitoring, and governance.

docs.title: Learning objectives

  • Security, availability, and operational visibility

docs.title: Real-world explanation
docs.text: In enterprise networking, Hub and Spoke is a core design pattern that improves scale, resilience, and control. In Azure, the equivalent service is represented as a managed platform component with APIs, policy, and integration points that make the service programmable rather than purely manual.

docs.title: Azure explanation
docs.text: Azure delivers VNets as a cloud-native building block. The design focus shifts from physical device management to policy, routing, service integration, and lifecycle automation.

docs.title: Networking engineer translation
docs.text: Think of VNets as the Azure equivalent of Hub & Spoke. The difference is that the controls live in the cloud control plane and are applied through Azure-native constructs rather than standalone appliances.

docs.title: Architecture diagram
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  A[Enterprise Edge] --> B[VNets]
  B --> C[Azure Resources]
  C --> D[Shared Services]

docs.title: Packet flow
docs.text:
1. A client request enters the Azure network boundary.
  2. The platform evaluates route and policy decisions.
  3. Traffic is forwarded to the destination resource or service.
  4. Return traffic follows the same policy-driven path.

docs.title: Portal walkthrough
docs.text:
1. Open the Azure portal.
  2. Create or review the relevant resource group and network object.
  3. Configure the service by selecting the appropriate SKU, region, and policy settings.
  4. Validate the deployment and inspect the metrics or logs.

docs.title: Highest-value facts
docs.text:
• NSGs are stateful and evaluate traffic at the subnet or NIC level.
  • User-defined routes override the system route table.
  • Azure Firewall is a stateful network firewall with built-in threat intelligence.
  • Private Endpoint gives private IP access to PaaS services.
  • ExpressRoute is a private circuit, not just a VPN.
  • Application Gateway is layer 7 and can terminate TLS.
  • Front Door is global edge and can route based on HTTP semantics.
  • Network Watcher is the operational toolbox for packet capture and flow logs.

docs.title: Common traps
docs.text:
• Confusing Private Link with VPN-based access
  • Assuming Azure routes are always the same as on-prem routing
  • Using a load balancer when you need an application delivery controller

docs.title: Decision tree
docs.text:
• Need private access to PaaS? Use Private Endpoint.
  • Need global edge routing? Use Front Door.
  • Need L7 inspection? Use Application Gateway.
  • Need stateful firewalling? Use Azure Firewall.

• Days 1–7: VNets, subnets, routing, NSGs, Azure Firewall
  • Days 8–14: Private Link, ExpressRoute, Virtual WAN, load balancing
  • Days 15–21: Front Door, Application Gateway, monitoring, and security
  • Days 22–27: Automation with Bicep, CLI, PowerShell, and labs
  • Days 28–30: Timed practice exams and final review

docs.title: 14-day plan
docs.text:
• Days 1–3: Core connectivity and routing
  • Days 4–6: Security and hybrid networking
  • Days 7–9: Application delivery and monitoring
  • Days 10–12: Automation and troubleshooting
  • Days 13–14: Review and mock exam

docs.title: Weekend cram
docs.text:
• Saturday: Review all comparison tables and flashcards
  • Sunday: Complete a timed practice set and inspect weak domains

docs.title: One-week review
docs.text:
• Revisit the exam cram guide and revisit every wrong answer
  • Rebuild the packet path for each service from memory

docs.title: Exam day checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm portal access if needed
  • Review the naming conventions and resource relationships
  • Bring a calm mindset and a plan for the first 15 minutes
